verdict.reasoning: Patient reports onset 2–3 days ago and exertional symptoms: "about two to three days ago I was running with a friend... I found myself actually short of breath" and ongoing "wheezing a bit and coughing. Just generally a bit short of breath."

Patient says: "about two to three days ago I was running with a friend... I found myself actually short of breath" and later "I'm not really short of breath when I'm walking, but definitely if I'm walking briskly now." This supports dyspnea with running and brisk walking.
Patient explicitly states: "I'm just wheezing a bit and coughing."
Patient: "I've used my blue inhaler, but to no avail. It hasn't really helped me." Blue inhaler is later identified as salbutamol.
Regarding Clenil (brown preventer): "I think I'm using that every day." and confirmed "Yes" to twice daily use.
Patient lists medications: "My history is salbutamol, Klenyl cetraben and hydrocortisone that I'm taking as well."
When asked about phlegm: "No, I don't. I'm not coughing up much sputum." indicating not producing substantial sputum.

Peak flow use: "Just every now and then. I haven't done over the last. Since I've had symptoms." and normal value is uncertain (initially "I think 130" then corrected by clinician), supporting infrequent use and unclear consistent readings.
When asked about last asthma review: "About two years ago."
Asthma is referred to repeatedly ("because your asthma was so bad?", "when was the last time you had an asthma attack?"), and patient answers consistently, implying a diagnosis of asthma.
Patient: "my sister has eczema and I've got a few issues that I think could be eczema as well." This suggests possible eczema history.
On allergies: "I have hay fever."
Use of blue inhaler: "I think just using that as and when I have symptoms." confirming PRN salbutamol use.
Preventer use: "I think I'm using that every day." and confirmed twice daily, consistent with daily brown preventer inhaler.
Patient medication list: "salbutamol, Klenyl cetraben and hydrocortisone that I'm taking as well."
Same list: "salbutamol, Klenyl cetraben and hydrocortisone that I'm taking as well."
Patient: "I have hay fever." and when asked about medication allergies: "Oh, no, sorry." The clinician confirms: "so you're not allergic to anything. Okay, so no allergies."
Family history: "My brother's asthmatic".
Same sentence: "My brother's asthmatic and my sister has eczema".
No occupational, smoking, alcohol, or other social history is discussed anywhere in the transcript, so stating that social history is not documented is accurate.
There are no vital signs (e.g., BP, HR, RR, SpO2) or physical exam findings recorded in the transcript.
A normal peak flow is discussed verbally ("Let's say it's about 380"), but no actual measured objective reading from this encounter is documented.

Clinician: "it looks like you can be having a small, small exacerbation" and patient has exertional "short of breath" with "wheezing a bit and coughing" that began "about two to three days ago" and worse over "just in the last two days."
Atopy history: patient has hay fever ("I have hay fever"), probable eczema ("issues that I think could be eczema"), and family history: "My brother's asthmatic and my sister has eczema."

Home monitoring: "Just every now and then. I haven't done over the last. Since I've had symptoms." plus initial uncertainty about baseline ("I think 130" then corrected by clinician), supporting incomplete monitoring and unclear baseline.
Clinician: "If you're using just two puffs twice a day, you can increase it to four puffs twice a day." referring to the brown inhaler (Clenil).
Clinician: "your salbutamol inhalers up to every two hourly" and earlier "Use it maximum about every two to four hours."

Clinician: "But if you're using it that often, that means too much that you know your asthma is really bad, you can use it, but that's not ideal." indicating frequent use is a marker of more severe symptoms needing evaluation.

Clinician: "if you're... using the asthma, you know, the blue inhalers every two to four hours. And your breathing's getting really worse. Then you would need to take yourself to A. E. You shouldn't wait for our appointment."
Clinician: "what I would like you to be seen by one of our GPS in the next few days" and later "Book an appointment... and I will recommend that you need a face to face."
Clinician: "when the doctor sees you, what we're going to do is we're going to examine your chest. Yeah. Make you do the peak reading."
Clinician: "So depending on what we find, you might need some antibiotics or some steroids." indicating possible short course of oral steroids or antibiotics.

Clinician emphasizes: "Then you would need to take yourself to A. E. You shouldn't wait for our appointment." and restated: "if your breathing's getting worse and you've not seen us, do take yourself to A E."
While preventer dose and frequency are discussed, there is no explicit instruction in the transcript about reviewing inhaler technique or adherence beyond dose change.
Clinician: "book an appointment, call support, Book an appointment to see, and I will recommend that you need a face to face." indicating the patient should arrange an appointment with their GP.

Clinician instructs to seek further care if symptoms worsen: "if your breathing's getting worse and you've not seen us, do take yourself to A E" and earlier emphasizing worsening symptoms with frequent inhaler use, which aligns with returning/escalating care if symptoms persist or worsen.
